title: Looking Back
objectives: I can use ten words to talk about the past, family history, and things we keep.
I can tell an antique, a relic, an heirloom, a keepsake, and a souvenir apart.
I can explain what a monument or a ceremony does when it commemorates something.
I can write about an object or a person's legacy using words from this unit.
rationale: History and family stories are full of objects and feelings that fifth graders can describe only as old stuff or missing the past. This unit gives them ten precise words that sort into three ideas: objects that carry memory (antique, relic, heirloom, keepsake, souvenir), public ways of remembering (commemorate, monument, legacy), and the feeling and the act of looking back (nostalgia, reminisce). The five object words overlap on purpose, so students learn to choose by how an object came to be kept: bought on a trip, treasured privately, passed down, or surviving from long ago. The passage uses an attic scene and a town ceremony so students can use the words in both a family and a community setting. Dignity, noble, and symbolize return because a monument or heirloom often symbolizes a value people consider noble.

passage.title: The Trunk in the Attic
paras: On a rainy Saturday, Nia and her great-uncle Tomas climbed into the attic to sort an old trunk. Inside lay an antique clock with a cracked face, a quilt wrapped in tissue, and a small tin box. "The quilt is an heirloom," Tomas said. "Four generations of our family have slept under it." He ran his hand over the stitches and began to reminisce about the winters he spent wrapped in it as a boy.

Nia opened the tin box. It held a paper ticket, a shell, and a tiny wooden horse. "Those are keepsakes," Tomas explained. "Your grandmother kept each one because it reminded her of someone she loved." He lifted the shell. "This is a souvenir from the seashore, the only trip she took with her sisters." A wave of nostalgia crossed his face, a warm and aching longing for days that were gone.

At the bottom of the trunk lay a rusty iron key. "A relic from the old mill," he said. "It opened the door of the building where our family worked for sixty years." Next week, the town would commemorate the mill's hundredth anniversary with a ceremony at the stone monument by the river, and Tomas planned to bring the key.

"Things are only part of our legacy," he said. "The bigger part is how we treated people and the work we left behind." Nia tucked the quilt around her knees and smiled. She could not wait to add her own story to the trunk.

qs.q: In paragraph 1, the word "heirloom" most nearly means
choices: a valuable object passed down through a family
a gift bought for a stranger
a tool for sewing a quilt
a broken object that is thrown away
qs.why: Tomas says four generations of the family have slept under the quilt, so an heirloom is a treasured object passed down in a family.

qs.q: Which detail best shows that the objects in the tin box are keepsakes?
choices: The tin box was at the bottom of the trunk.
The ticket was made of paper.
Nia's grandmother kept each one to remind her of someone she loved.
The wooden horse was very small.
qs.why: Tomas explains that each object was kept because it reminded Nia's grandmother of someone she loved, which is what a keepsake does.

qs.q: What does the author mean by "a wave of nostalgia crossed his face"?
choices: He felt a warm, aching longing for the past.
He suddenly became seasick.
He was angry about the shell.
He was bored by the stories.
qs.why: The next phrase describes a warm and aching longing for days that were gone, which is what nostalgia means.

qs.q: Why does Tomas plan to bring the key to the ceremony?
choices: The key opens the stone monument.
The key is a relic from the mill that the town is honoring.
He wants to sell the key to the town.
Nia asked him to bring it.
qs.why: The ceremony commemorates the mill's anniversary, and the key is a relic from the mill, so it connects to what the town is honoring.

qs.q: Which sentence best states the main idea of the passage?
choices: Antiques are always worth more than souvenirs.
Old attics are dangerous places to explore.
Objects hold family memories, but the people and values behind them matter most.
The town should build a new monument.
qs.why: Tomas shows the objects and their stories, then says things are only part of a legacy and how we treated people is the bigger part.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words about memory and the past, from objects they can hold to ideas they can feel. The attic and ceremony passage lets them hear the words in family and town settings. Writing asks students to describe an object and the memory it carries, then to think about what people leave behind.

notes.va.reminisce.v: Reminisce is a verb: people reminisce, usually together and fondly. Contrast with remember, which can be neutral. Model by telling a short, happy story about a childhood object.
notes.va.commemorate.v: Commemorate means to honor the memory of something, usually in public. Students may confuse it with celebrate. A moment of silence commemorates; a party celebrates. Have students list ways a community commemorates.
notes.va.relic.n: A relic survives from a much earlier time. Keep the taught sense of an old surviving object. Some students know relic only from religion or adventure movies, so say that it is the broader sense here.
notes.va.antique.n: Antiques are valued for their age, and age is part of the definition. Stress that old is not enough: an antique is valued, usually over a hundred years old. Clarify the noun sense: an antique is an object, and antique is also an adjective, as in an antique clock.
notes.va.heirloom.n: Students may think any old thing is an heirloom. The key idea is passed down within a family. Ask who would receive the object next. Pair with legacy: an heirloom is one object, a legacy can be much bigger.
notes.va.monument.n: Monument is a public marker, such as a statue or a stone. Students may think of famous national monuments only. Have them find a local marker and ask what it commemorates.
notes.va.nostalgia.n: Nostalgia is a feeling, not an object or an event. It is often sweet and sad at once, which links to the bittersweet word students meet in unit 20. Ask students what sounds or smells bring it on.
notes.va.keepsake.n: A keepsake is small and personal, chosen by the owner. Contrast with souvenir, which is tied to a place visited, and with heirloom, which is tied to a family line. One object can be more than one, so ask students to explain their sort.
notes.va.souvenir.n: A souvenir marks a place you visited. It is usually bought or collected on the trip. The word comes from French, where it can also mean a memory, which helps students remember the meaning. Compare with keepsake.
notes.va.legacy.n: Legacy is what a person leaves behind for the future, and it can be things, values, or achievements. Students often think legacy means money only. Ask them to describe the legacy of someone they admire.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'Tomas says the quilt is an heirloom. The text says four generations have slept under it, so it has been passed down in the family. A souvenir is bought on a trip, so the quilt is not a souvenir. The shell is a souvenir because it came from a seashore trip. I can check each word against a clue in the text.'
